name: TLV9301IDBVR
title: 40 V, 1 MHz rail-to-rail-output operational amplifiers (single, dual, quad)
summary: TLV9301, TLV9302 and TLV9304 are one, two and four general-purpose op amps for supplies from 4.5 V to 40 V. The output swings to within millivolts of each rail; the input range reaches 100 mV below V– and stops 2 V short of V+ for full performance. Gain-bandwidth is 1 MHz, slew rate 3 V/µs, quiescent current 150 µA per channel, and the inputs tolerate the full supply between them, so the part also serves as a comparator.

circuits.title: Single-pole low-pass filter with gain
circuits.description: R1 and C1 form a first-order RC low-pass at the non-inverting input; the amplifier then buffers that node with a non-inverting gain of 1 + RF / RG. The corner sits at 1 / (2π R1 C1).

circuits.title: Buffer driving 100 Ω into thermal shutdown
circuits.description: A unity-gain follower on a single 30 V supply holds 3 V across a 100 Ω load, so it sources 30 mA and dissipates 0.81 W. At TA = 65°C with RθJA = 138.7°C/W the junction would reach 177.3°C; instead the output turns off above 140°C, the load pulls the output to 0 V, the die cools, and the output cycles between 3 V and 0 V.

circuits.title: Follower with an isolation resistor for capacitive loads
circuits.description: A unity-gain follower on split supplies takes its feedback from the amplifier pin, ahead of RISO, and drives a capacitive load through RISO. RISO, typically 10 Ω to 20 Ω, cuts ringing and lifts phase margin while keeping DC accuracy into a purely capacitive load; any resistive load in parallel forms a divider with RISO and adds a gain error in proportion to RISO / RL.

circuits.title: Non-inverting amplifier with TVS clamps on the supplies
circuits.description: A non-inverting amplifier (gain set by RF and R1, input through RS, load RL) on split supplies, with a TVS diode from each supply rail to ground. During an ESD or overstress event the part's internal steering diodes carry input or output current into the supply lines; the TVS diodes hold the rails down so the internal absorption cell is not driven in-circuit, and RS limits the input current.
notes: The part's input pins each pass through an internal 100 Ω resistor.

circuits.title: 40 V precision comparator
circuits.description: The amplifier runs open loop as a comparator on a single 40 V supply. R1 and R2 split V+ to make a 20 V threshold at the inverting input; the input drives the non-inverting input, so the output goes to the positive rail when VIN is above 20 V and to the negative rail when it is below. The wide differential input range allows the inputs to sit far apart. Larger resistors save power; smaller ones lower noise.

circuits.title: Non-inverting amplifier with supply bypassing
circuits.description: A non-inverting amplifier with gain 1 + RF / RG on split supplies, each supply pin bypassed to ground by a low-ESR 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor placed close to the part. RF and RG sit close to the inverting input to keep its parasitic capacitance low.
notes: With a single supply one capacitor from V+ to ground is enough.

equations.name: Low-pass filter transfer function
equations.expr: VOUT / VIN = (1 + RF / RG) × 1 / (1 + s R1 C1)

where.RG: resistor from the inverting input to ground
where.C1: capacitor from the non-inverting input to ground

where.θJA: junction-to-ambient thermal resistance, 138.7°C/W in the thermal-protection example
where.PD: power dissipated, 0.81 W in the example

operation.text: TLV9301 holds one amplifier, TLV9302 two and TLV9304 four. They run from 4.5 V to 40 V (±2.25 V to ±20 V), have a rail-to-rail output, 1 MHz gain-bandwidth, 3 V/µs slew rate, ±0.5 mV typical offset with ±2 µV/°C drift, ±60 mA output current and 150 µA quiescent current per amplifier, and are specified from –40°C to 125°C.
TLV9304-Q1 is an automotive version of TLV9304 qualified to AEC-Q100.

The inputs carry no back-to-back protection diodes between them. The differential voltage between the two inputs may go up to the full 40 V supply without the inputs drawing extra current, so fast input steps (from a multiplexer, for instance) settle without the distortion and delay that diode clamps cause, and the part can be used as a comparator.
Filtering on chip reduces the effect of RF interference. EMIRR at the non-inverting input is measured from 10 MHz to 6 GHz; it is about 72 dB at 1 GHz.
Driving the inputs past the rails does not reverse the output; the output stays limited at the matching rail.
The absolute maximum junction temperature is 150°C. A temperature sensor turns the output drive off above 140°C, leaving the output high impedance until the die cools, after which it drives again.

The output stage is resistive and drives small capacitive loads directly; higher closed-loop gain allows more capacitance. For larger loads at unity gain a series resistor RISO of 10 Ω to 20 Ω between the output and the load keeps the loop stable. The capacitive-load drive suits reference buffers, MOSFET gate drive and cable-shield drive.

The input works from 100 mV below V– to within 2 V of V+ with full performance, on a P-channel pair. An N-channel pair in parallel takes over from about (V+) – 1 V up to 100 mV above V+, and both pairs conduct from about (V+) – 2 V to (V+) – 1 V; the edges of this region shift with process. Above (V+) – 2 V offset, drift, CMRR, PSRR, noise and THD are worse.

Steering diodes run from each input and the output to the internal supply lines, where an absorption cell clamps the supplies during an ESD event. They protect the part out of circuit (handling, assembly, test); an ESD event is short and high voltage (around 1 kV for 100 ns), an overstress event long and lower (around 50 V for 100 ms). Turning the absorption cell on in a powered circuit can cause damage; series resistors that limit current, together with TVS diodes on the rails, let the internal diodes survive overstress.
When the output saturates, it needs about 1 µs to come back to linear operation, and then slews at the normal rate. The delay out of overload is that recovery time plus the slew time.

A typical value for a quantity with a non-zero mean (gain-bandwidth, for instance) is the mean. For a quantity centred near zero (offset voltage) it is the mean plus one standard deviation. With 500 µV typical offset, about 68% of parts lie within ±500 µV, and at 4σ (±2000 µV) about 0.0063% lie outside. Parts beyond a min or max limit are screened out, so the 2.5 mV offset limit holds although it is near 5σ. From the drift distribution and its 2 µV/°C typical, 6σ for offset drift is about 12 µV/°C; a value with no limit carries no guarantee.
There is one mode: the part operates above a 4.5 V (±2.25 V) supply, and 40 V (±20 V) is the most it is specified for; supplies above 40 V can damage it.
Each supply pin wants a low-ESR 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor to ground right at the part; on a single supply one capacitor from V+ to ground is enough.

Keep analog and digital grounds apart and follow the ground current paths; a ground plane spreads heat and lowers EMI pickup. Route inputs away from supply and output traces, crossing at right angles where they must cross, and keep input traces short. Put RF and RG next to the inverting input. A driven low-impedance guard ring round sensitive traces lowers leakage. Clean the board after assembly; after an aqueous wash, bake at 85°C for 30 minutes to drive moisture out of the package.
